steps: The digestive system breaks down complex food into simple, soluble substances that can be absorbed into the blood.
The absorbed nutrients are transported to body cells and used for energy, growth and repair.
Undigested food is removed from the body as faeces; this helps prevent unwanted material from accumulating.
The excretory system removes metabolic wastes from the body.
The kidneys filter the blood and remove urea, excess water and salts to form urine.
By regulating the amount of water and salts in the body and removing wastes, these systems help maintain a stable internal environment.
items.finalAnswer: The digestive system supplies useful nutrients, while the excretory system removes wastes and regulates water and salts; together they help maintain homeostasis.

steps: Roots anchor the plant in the soil and absorb water and mineral salts.
The stem supports the plant and bears leaves, flowers and fruits.
The stem transports water and mineral salts from the roots to the leaves, and food from the leaves to other parts of the plant.
Leaves make food by photosynthesis; they also exchange gases and lose water vapour through transpiration.
Flowers are the reproductive organs of flowering plants. They produce seeds, often enclosed in fruits.
Fruits protect seeds and help in their dispersal.
items.finalAnswer: Roots absorb and anchor, stems support and transport, leaves make food, and flowers and fruits take part in reproduction and seed dispersal.

steps: The root system consists of all the roots of a plant and usually grows below the ground.
It anchors the plant firmly in the soil and absorbs water and mineral salts.
The root tip is protected by a root cap as it pushes through the soil.
Behind the root cap is the region of cell division, where new cells are produced.
In the region of elongation, cells increase in length and push the root tip farther into the soil.
In the region of maturation, cells differentiate into specialised tissues; root hairs increase the surface area for absorption.
The cortex lies inside the outer layer of the root and stores food and allows water to pass inward.
The central vascular tissues contain xylem, which transports water and mineral salts, and phloem, which transports food.
items.finalAnswer: The root system anchors the plant, absorbs water and mineral salts, and contains tissues that transport materials through the plant.

steps: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment of the body.
It is important because body cells and enzymes function properly only within suitable internal conditions.
The digestive system supplies nutrients, and the respiratory system supplies oxygen and removes carbon dioxide.
The circulatory system transports oxygen, nutrients, hormones and wastes between body parts.
The excretory system removes metabolic wastes and helps regulate water and salts in the body.
The nervous and endocrine systems coordinate the activities of organs and help regulate body conditions.
These organ systems work together to keep the internal environment stable despite changes inside or outside the body.
items.finalAnswer: Homeostasis is the maintenance of a constant internal environment, achieved through the coordinated work of the body’s organ systems.

steps: The respiratory system brings oxygen into the lungs and removes carbon dioxide from the body.
In the alveoli of the lungs, oxygen diffuses into the blood and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the air.
The circulatory system transports oxygen in the blood from the lungs to body cells.
Body cells use oxygen during cellular respiration and produce carbon dioxide as a waste product.
The blood carries carbon dioxide from the cells to the lungs, where it diffuses into the alveoli and is breathed out.
By working together, the respiratory and circulatory systems supply oxygen and remove carbon dioxide, helping maintain homeostasis.
items.finalAnswer: The respiratory system exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide in the lungs, while the circulatory system carries these gases between the lungs and body cells.

steps: Epithelial tissue covers the body surface, lines internal organs and cavities, and forms glands.
Its cells are closely packed, with very little space between them, forming a protective covering or lining.
The shape and arrangement of epithelial cells vary according to their function and location.
Thin, flat epithelial cells allow rapid diffusion and are found where exchange occurs, such as in the air sacs of the lungs.
In places exposed to wear and tear, several layers of epithelial cells provide protection.
Some epithelial cells are specialised for absorption or secretion; for example, the lining of the intestine absorbs digested food.
items.finalAnswer: The closely packed cells of epithelial tissue form coverings and linings, while their shapes and arrangements suit protection, exchange, absorption or secretion.

steps: Organ systems work in harmony to carry out the functions needed to keep the body alive and maintain homeostasis.
Each system depends on other systems; for example, the respiratory system supplies oxygen, while the circulatory system carries it to cells.
The circulatory system also carries nutrients from the digestive system and wastes to the excretory system.
Failure of one organ system can disturb the functions of other systems because materials may not be supplied or removed properly.
For example, failure of the respiratory system reduces oxygen supply and prevents efficient removal of carbon dioxide; this affects cellular respiration and can damage other organs.
Failure of the circulatory system prevents oxygen, nutrients and wastes from being transported effectively throughout the body.
Therefore, the coordinated functioning of all organ systems is essential for survival and for maintaining a stable internal environment.
items.finalAnswer: Organ systems are interdependent; failure of one can disrupt other systems and disturb homeostasis, so their coordinated functioning is essential for survival.
